title: Single-Implementation Traits Without a Present Abstraction Purpose
pattern: A trait and its only concrete implementer duplicate an interface without a current polymorphic, decoupling, or testing purpose, creating a just-in-case abstraction.
why_bad: An unnecessary extra interface adds indirection that complicates navigation, compilation, and coordinated changes without buying interchangeable behavior or isolation. It directly violates YAGNI.
detection: Count implementations in production and test code and inspect usage. A trait declaration with exactly one `impl` block across production and test code is the candidate signal; a trait whose method surface exactly matches its single implementer, with no polymorphic usage (no `dyn Trait`, no generic bound on it), is the narrower confirmed case. Confirm that no present package boundary, consumer extension contract, or required abstraction purpose justifies the trait before recommending removal.
counterexample: Explicit boundaries between packages to isolate unstable third-party code; complex or nondeterministic I/O boundaries (email or SMS gateways, external systems) where a fake/mock is required in tests; and an actual abstraction or external implementation contract even when only one implementation is visible locally.
fix: When the trait has no present purpose beyond the concrete type, apply Collapse Hierarchy: move behavior to the concrete struct as needed, migrate consumers to depend on it directly, and remove the redundant trait. Retain purposeful boundaries instead of inferring obsolescence from a local implementation count.
source: Fowler, *Refactoring*, Chapter 3 ("Speculative Generality - Collapse Hierarchy"); Martin Fowler, *Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture* (2002), p. 245; Steve McConnell, *Code Complete* (2004), Chapter 24.
